findings.evidence: Stars form in dense regions of cold interstellar gas and dust clouds when gravity overcomes support from pressure, turbulence and magnetic fields.
A collapsing core heats and accretes gas, often through a disk; outflows and jets remove some material and angular momentum.
A star reaches the main sequence after its core becomes hot and dense enough for sustained hydrogen fusion to balance inward gravity.
Dust can obscure young stars in visible light; infrared and radio observations reveal embedded protostars, gas and disks.

findings.claim: Not all cloud becomes one star
findings.evidence: Clouds fragment into multiple dense cores, and feedback from young stars can disperse or reshape remaining gas.

editorial_angles: Separate the cloud, dense core, protostar and main-sequence star stages.
Explain collapse as a competition between gravity and support, not a guaranteed event for every cloud.
Describe accretion disks and outflows as a way to move mass and angular momentum.
Clarify that hydrogen fusion marks a major transition but star formation is not instantaneous.
Explain why observations combine visible, infrared, radio and X-ray data.
